title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
description: At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.Firef
body: At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause. Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning. Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.

schema.headline: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory

title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
description: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.A string of black and white photos shared
body: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.The American singer confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia."I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret."We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.The singer, whose hits include Party in the U.S.A and Wrecking Ball, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

schema.headline: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony

title: Flights cancelled in Belgium due to cost-of-living strike
description: Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measu
body: Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate. No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. "In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled."Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels."Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition. One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse. "While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system". Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes". "Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

schema.headline: Flights cancelled in Belgium due to cost-of-living strike

title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
description: A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).The hair once belonged to John G
body: A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.Its new owner has not been named. Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website. McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms. Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum. "Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction. In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

schema.headline: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000

title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
description: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filin
body: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows."To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days."There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant  will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states. It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place. Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible. Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen."There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement. The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing. The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

schema.headline: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order

title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Can
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney. "We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress. "I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala. He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians."I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration. The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump. They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., externalCritch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel."Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

schema.headline: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner

title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
description: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when
body: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, had been missing for more than a year.Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight."She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue."He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen"."She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did."That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent."Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina."And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025. He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.But she kept any of those fears from Jenny."I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door."I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.He remains behind bars awaiting trial.A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her."Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away.""She's doing great for what she's gone through."They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen."I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

schema.headline: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl

title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
description: Figure caption, Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent says party needs to 'bring change'ByMadeline HalpertUpdated 6 hours agoThe D
body: Figure caption, Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent says party needs to 'bring change'ByMadeline HalpertUpdated 6 hours agoThe Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called. Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats. View the 2026 midterm election resultsSunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%."I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable. Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of RepresentativesHubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx two years ago by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa. Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters. Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website. The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes. Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law. However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation. Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat

title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah visit: India to give $1.62bn economic package
description: Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the I
body: Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.The contrast between the two leaders was striking. Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor. Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths. India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old. His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs."Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.There was, however, disappointment on aviation.Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects."The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional."Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

schema.headline: Nepal PM Balendra Shah visit: India to give $1.62bn economic package

title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
description: Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the
body: Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity."In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn."Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking."It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn."Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory."The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

schema.headline: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing

title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
description: Image source, Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of ex
body: Image source, Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)ByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemUpdated 2 hours agoGaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says, external.Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards". Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contaminationOxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials."There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been clearedWith all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent campsAlready, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps."There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."Image caption, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the warFarmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe."Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

schema.headline: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failureByClim
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failureByClimate EditorSome may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty."For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.The wider political backdrop was still more revealing. The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.A majority that may yet offer hopeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action. So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received."This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the COP processSo is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary. Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.Figure caption, What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?A rare moment of agreementPerhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

schema.headline: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world

title: 'Chapo Isidro': Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
description: Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sin
body: Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state. The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday. In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age. It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets. The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico"."For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013. According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state. The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

schema.headline: 'Chapo Isidro': Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest

title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
description: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities
body: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom."We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said."The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari."Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

schema.headline: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say

title: Nigeria boat accident: At least 29 dead after overcrowded boat capsizes in Bayelsa
description: Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.T
body: Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services."As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News."Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets."Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access."Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

schema.headline: Nigeria boat accident: At least 29 dead after overcrowded boat capsizes in Bayelsa
